title: Get Well Soon in Spanish: Messages and Phrases

meta_description: Get well soon in Spanish: que te mejores, recupérate pronto, messages for friends, family, colleagues and after surgery, plus how to ask how someone feels.
excerpt: Que te mejores: kind words for when someone you care about is ill.

body_html:
Get well soon in Spanish is usually ¡Que te mejores!, a short, warm phrase you’ll hear everywhere from Madrid to Mexico City. But when someone you care about is ill, you may want to say more: ask how they feel, offer help or send a thoughtful message. This guide gives you the words for colds and flu, hospital stays, surgery and longer illnesses, for friends, family and colleagues, in both informal and formal Spanish.

Key takeaways
  • ¡Que te mejores! is the standard “get well soon” (que se mejore with usted).
  • Recupérate pronto and Pronta recuperación are common in messages.
  • Ask with ¿Cómo te encuentras? or ¿Qué tal estás?
  • Offering help is often more meaningful than any phrase.
{{toc}}

Get well soon in Spanish: the main phrases

SpanishEnglishRegister
¡Que te mejores!Get well soon!Informal (tú)
¡Que se mejore!Get well soon!Formal (usted)
¡Recupérate pronto!Recover soon!Informal
Te deseo una pronta recuperación.I wish you a speedy recovery.Neutral, cards
¡Mejórate!Get better!Informal, short
Cuídate mucho.Take good care of yourself.Warm

Que te mejores uses the subjunctive to express a wish, like que tengas un buen día. The RAE dictionary lists “to recover health” among the meanings of mejorar.

Asking how someone feels

  • ¿Cómo te encuentras? How are you feeling?
  • ¿Qué tal estás hoy? How are you today?
  • ¿Estás mejor? Are you feeling better?
  • ¿Qué te ha dicho el médico? What did the doctor say?
  • Me he enterado de que estás malo. ¿Necesitas algo? I heard you’re ill. Do you need anything?

For describing symptoms yourself, see {{link:at-the-doctor-in-spanish|at the doctor in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Messages for friends and family

  • ¡Que te mejores pronto! Te echo de menos en el trabajo. Get well soon! I miss you at work.
  • Mucho ánimo. Pronto estarás como nuevo. Hang in there. You’ll be as good as new soon.
  • Descansa y no te preocupes por nada. Rest and don’t worry about anything.
  • Si necesitas algo, aquí estoy. If you need anything, I’m here.
  • Te mando un abrazo enorme. Sending you a huge hug.

After surgery or a hospital stay

  • Me alegro de que la operación haya salido bien. I’m glad the operation went well.
  • Tómate el tiempo que necesites para recuperarte. Take all the time you need to recover.
  • ¿Puedo ir a verte al hospital? Can I come and visit you in hospital?
  • Paso a paso. Lo estás haciendo muy bien. Step by step. You’re doing really well.
{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Formal messages for colleagues

For a boss, client or older person, use usted: Le deseo una pronta recuperación, Espero que se mejore pronto, No se preocupe por el trabajo; lo tenemos todo cubierto. A team card might say: De parte de todo el equipo, te deseamos que te recuperes pronto. ¡Te esperamos! (From the whole team, we hope you recover soon. We’re waiting for you!) See {{link:talking-to-coworkers-in-spanish|talking to coworkers in Spanish}}.

For longer or serious illnesses

When someone faces a long illness, avoid promising that everything will be fine. Gentle, present-focused phrases are kinder: Pienso mucho en ti (I think about you a lot), Estoy contigo en todo esto (I’m with you through all of this), No tienes que contestar; solo quería que supieras que te quiero (You don’t have to reply; I just wanted you to know I love you). Practical help, such as ¿Te llevo la comida el jueves? (Shall I bring you food on Thursday?), often matters more than words. More in {{link:how-to-comfort-someone-in-spanish|how to comfort someone in Spanish}}.

A sample conversation

  • A: Hola, Marta. Me ha dicho Luis que tienes gripe. ¿Cómo te encuentras? (Hi Marta. Luis told me you have flu. How are you feeling?)
  • B: Fatal, la verdad. Tengo fiebre y me duele todo. (Awful, honestly. I have a fever and everything hurts.)
  • A: ¡Pobre! Descansa mucho. ¿Te llevo algo de la farmacia? (Poor thing! Rest lots. Shall I bring you something from the pharmacy?)
  • B: Eres un sol, gracias. (You’re a star, thanks.)
  • A: De nada. ¡Que te mejores!

Regional expressions

In Spain, people often say someone está malo or está pachucho (feeling a bit rough), and wish them ¡Que te mejores!. In Mexico and much of Latin America, está enfermo is more common, and you might hear ¡Que te alivies! (literally “may you be relieved”), a very warm, everyday way to say get well soon. In Argentina, ¡Que te mejores pronto! and ¡Fuerza! (Stay strong!) are typical. Any of these shows care, and que te mejores is understood everywhere.

Gifts and visits

When visiting someone who is ill at home or in hospital, it is common to bring something small: fruit, chocolates, a magazine or flowers. Ask first: ¿Quieres que pase a verte? (Would you like me to drop by?) and keep visits short: No quiero cansarte, me voy ya (I don’t want to tire you out, I’ll go now).

Final thoughts

A simple ¡Que te mejores! goes a long way, and a message that adds Si necesitas algo, aquí estoy goes even further. Choose tú or usted, keep it warm, and offer real help when you can. For more everyday situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you say “get well soon” in Spanish?
faq.a: ¡Que te mejores! (informal) or ¡Que se mejore! (formal). You can also say ¡Recupérate pronto! or Te deseo una pronta recuperación.

faq.q: How do you ask someone how they feel in Spanish?
faq.a: ¿Cómo te encuentras?, ¿Qué tal estás hoy? or ¿Estás mejor?

faq.q: What do you write in a get-well card in Spanish?
faq.a: Te deseo una pronta recuperación. Descansa mucho y, si necesitas algo, aquí estoy. Un abrazo enorme.
